title: Elin and the Color Chaos
markdown:
The sun burst open, painting the sky gold and pink. Elin rocketed out of bed, notepad ready. Today was the Spectrum Spectacular — art meeting science in a hall that usually smelled of varnish and nerves. Bramble the seal pup flipped in the pool, barking, “Colours! But why, Elin, why?”

Dr. Ada Brook, curator extraordinaire, burst in, already mid-disaster. “The Colour Creation Station is kaput!” She tripped on a cable that had no business in a doorway. “It’s supposed to show how we see colour. The screens are dull grey. We open in two hours.”

They dashed. Wires tangled like guilty spaghetti. Screens blinked grey, then greyer, a talent. “They mixed paint logic with light logic,” Brook groaned. “Pigments on a light-screen. Mud. Institutional mud.”

Elin’s mind clicked. “Paint takes away colours. Subtractive. Screens add light. Additive.”

Bramble chased a sunbeam across the wet tiles, batting. “Bending! Bouncing!”

“Exactly. Light adds. Screens use tiny emitters to trick the eye. This machine is mixing red and green paint on a screen and calling it a lesson. That’s why it’s mud.”

She rerouted wires, separating light emitters from pigment displays, muttering at whoever had labelled both jacks IN in the same cheerful font. She set up a separate table for actual paints, jars uncapped, brushes that had survived worse exhibitions. “Watch.” She projected red light and green light onto a white board. Brilliant yellow burst forth, clean as a shout.

Then she mixed red paint with blue. A deep purple bloomed, a different kind of victory, thicker, slower.

The main screens flickered, then flared. A kaleidoscope: reds, greens, blues dancing, every shade the additive set could invent. The pigment jars gleamed on their own table, honest about what they subtracted. It worked. A guest who had arrived early clapped, then looked embarrassed, then clapped again.

“You fixed it,” Brook said, less shriek than last time. “Brilliant.”

Elin did not offer two colour secrets for the universe. “Light adds, brighter. Paint mixes, takes away. Do not plug them into the same box and hope.”

Bramble barked and did a celebratory flip that sprinkled the pigment table; Elin moved the yellow jar in time. Understanding why was the useful part. Brook ushered guests toward the yellow-from-light demo first, the purple-from-paint second, a sequence that would save her the mud speech.

Elin grinned, a spark, and did not declare the adventure begun. She taped a card above each station — ADD and TAKE AWAY — in letters even a hurried intern could not mix up, wiped seal-water off the board, and let Bramble keep the sunbeam, which had been, after all, the first correct demonstration of the day.
